summary: Updates RFC 3370 to describe how to use the SHAKE family of hash functions in the Cryptographic Message Syntax with RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA. It also describes conventions for the associated signer public keys.

plainLanguage.summary: SHAKE is a hash function whose output length the caller chooses, which makes it useful where the old hash functions do not fit. This RFC says how to use it inside CMS, the format for signed and encrypted mail, and fixes the one thing that has to be pinned down: how long the output should be in each place it is used.

subtitle: How to sign and authenticate mail with the SHAKE hash functions in Cryptographic Message Syntax.

tldr.problem: CMS, the format used for signed and encrypted mail, has an algorithms document that lists which hash and signature algorithms may be used. The SHA-3 family of hash functions was not in that list, and the two extendable-output functions in that family need extra care because their output length has to be fixed by the surrounding algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds eight object identifiers covering SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 as message digests, as the hash inside RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA signatures, and inside the KMAC message authentication code, and it fixes the output length each use must have: 32 bytes for SHAKE128 and 64 bytes for SHAKE256.
tldr.outcome: CMS implementations now have standard identifiers and unambiguous rules for using SHAKE, including the salt length and mask generation function settings that RSASSA-PSS requires, and the recommendation of which key sizes go with which hash.

facts.label: PSS salt length
facts.value: 32 bytes for SHAKE128 and 64 bytes for SHAKE256

today: RFC 8702 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2020. It updates RFC 3370, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. The identifiers it uses for the signatures themselves come from RFC 8692.

sections.title: What SHAKE Brings to CMS
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax describes the syntax used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message contents. The separate CMS Algorithms document defines the use of common cryptographic algorithms with CMS. This specification updates that algorithms document and describes the use of SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 as new hash functions in CMS, together with their use with the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm with the CMS signed-data content type.

In the SHA-3 family, two extendable-output functions are defined, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256, along with four other hash function instances that are out of scope for this document. A SHAKE is a variable-length hash function defined as SHAKE(M, d), where the output is a d-bit-long digest of the message M. The collision and second-preimage-resistance strengths for SHAKE128 are min(d/2,128) and min(d,128) bits, and for SHAKE256 they are min(d/2,256) and min(d,256) bits. This specification uses d=256 for SHAKE128 and d=512 for SHAKE256.

A SHAKE can be used in CMS as the message digest function, that is, to hash the message that is to be signed, in RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA, as the message authentication code, and as the mask generation function in RSASSA-PSS.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual hash functions always produce a fixed length, such as 32 bytes. SHAKE lets the caller choose the length, which is what makes it useful here, but it also means every use has to say how long it wants. This RFC fixes those lengths.

sections.title: The Object Identifiers
sections.content:
The section identifies eight new object identifiers for using SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 in CMS. Two of them are for the hash functions themselves: id-shake128 and id-shake256. When either is used, the parameters MUST be absent, so the identifier is a SEQUENCE of one component, the object identifier itself.

Two further identifiers are for RSASSA-PSS signatures using the SHAKEs, id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128 and id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256, and two more for ECDSA signatures using the SHAKEs, id-ecdsa-with-shake128 and id-ecdsa-with-shake256. The parameters for these four MUST also be absent. The same RSASSA-PSS algorithm identifiers can be used for identifying public keys and signatures.

The last two identifiers are for the Keccak message authentication codes using SHAKE128 and SHAKE256. For these, the parameters are OPTIONAL. The parameters field carries the length of the requested output and the customization string; when it is absent, the SHAKE output length used in KMAC is 32 or 64 bytes respectively and the customization string is an empty string by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Each use of a hash function is named by a number that software recognises. There are eight such numbers here, one for each combination of function and purpose. Most of them must carry no extra information at all, because the rules are fixed in the specification.

sections.title: Message Digests
sections.content:
The id-shake128 and id-shake256 object identifiers can be used as the digest algorithm identifiers located in the SignedData, SignerInfo, DigestedData and AuthenticatedData digestAlgorithm fields in CMS. The encoding of the identifier MUST omit the parameters field and the output length of SHAKE128 or SHAKE256, because the message digest MUST be 32 or 64 bytes respectively.

The digest values are located in the DigestedData field and in the Message Digest authenticated attribute included in the signedAttributes of the SignedData signerInfos. Digest values are also input to the signature algorithms, and the digest algorithm MUST be the same as the message hash algorithms used in the signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message is hashed for signing, the hash is 32 bytes with SHAKE128 and 64 bytes with SHAKE256. The length is not written into the message, because it is fixed by the rules, so the identifier carries no extra information.

sections.title: Signatures with SHAKE
sections.content:
Conforming implementations that process RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA with SHAKE signatures MUST recognize the corresponding identifiers. When using RSASSA-PSS or ECDSA with the SHAKEs, the RSA modulus or ECDSA curve order SHOULD be chosen in line with the SHAKE output length.

For RSASSA-PSS, the encoding MUST omit the parameters field, because the hash, mask generation algorithm, trailer and salt are embedded in the identifier definition rather than carried as parameters. The hash algorithm used to hash the message being signed and the hash algorithm used as the mask generation function MUST be the same, both SHAKE128 or both SHAKE256, and the output length of the hash algorithm that hashes the message SHALL be 32 bytes for SHAKE128 or 64 bytes for SHAKE256.

The SHAKEs MUST be used natively as the mask generation function, instead of the MGF1 algorithm that uses the hash function in multiple iterations. The mask generation function output length is emLen - hLen - 1 bytes, where emLen is the maximum message length ceil((n-1)/8) for an RSA modulus n in bits, and hLen is 32 or 64 bytes. So when SHAKE is used as the mask generation function, the SHAKE output length is (8*emLen - 264) or (8*emLen - 520) bits respectively. With an RSA modulus of 2048, the output length is 1784 or 1528 bits. The RSASSA-PSS saltLength MUST be 32 bytes for id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128 or 64 bytes for id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256, and the trailerField MUST be 1, which represents the trailer field with hexadecimal value 0xBC.

For ECDSA, the respective SHAKE function is used as the hash and the parameters field MUST be omitted. For simplicity and compliance with the ECDSA standard, the output length of the hash function must be explicitly determined: 32 bytes for SHAKE128 and 64 bytes for SHAKE256. Certification authorities that generate ECDSA with SHAKE signatures SHOULD generate them with a deterministically generated, nonrandom k in accordance with RFC 6979, and may generate them under the other recommendations of the ECDSA standards if they have a stated policy requiring conformance to them, since those standards do not list SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 as hash options.
sections.plainLanguage: For RSA signatures the RFC fixes the salt at 32 or 64 bytes, matching the hash, and uses the hash directly to make the mask instead of running it repeatedly. For elliptic curve signatures the hash length is fixed at 32 or 64 bytes and the signing nonce should be derived deterministically rather than at random.

sections.title: Public Keys
sections.content:
In CMS the signer's public key algorithm identifiers are located in the OriginatorPublicKey algorithm attribute, and the conventions and encoding for RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA public key algorithm identifiers are as specified in the relevant PKIX documents.

Traditionally the rsaEncryption object identifier is used to identify RSA public keys, and it continues to do so when the RSA private key owner does not wish to limit the use of the public key exclusively to RSASSA-PSS with the SHAKEs. When the owner does want to limit the key to RSASSA-PSS, the RSASSA-PSS algorithm identifier SHOULD be used as the algorithm attribute in the OriginatorPublicKey sequence. Conforming implementations that process RSASSA-PSS with SHAKE public keys in CMS messages MUST recognize the corresponding identifiers, and conforming implementations MUST specify and process the algorithms explicitly using those identifiers when encoding ECDSA with SHAKE public keys. The identifier parameters MUST be absent.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key that goes with the signature is labelled in the same way. An RSA key can be labelled in the ordinary RSA way, which leaves it usable for other purposes, or labelled strictly as an RSASSA-PSS key, which restricts it. An elliptic curve key must always be labelled explicitly.

sections.title: Message Authentication Codes
sections.content:
The Keccak message authentication code is specified in a NIST publication. In CMS the KMAC algorithm identifiers are located in the AuthenticatedData macAlgorithm field, and the KMAC values are located in the AuthenticatedData mac field.

When the id-KmacWithSHAKE128 or id-KmacWithSHAKE256 identifier is used as the MAC algorithm identifier, the parameters field is optional, either absent or present. If absent, the SHAKE output length used in KMAC is 32 or 64 bytes respectively and the customization string is an empty string by default. Conforming implementations that process KMACs with the SHAKEs MUST recognize these identifiers.

When calculating the KMAC output, the variable N is 0xD2B282C2, S is an empty string, and L, the integer representing the requested output length in bits, is 256 or 512 for the two identifiers respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: For the keyed version of the hash, the same identifiers are used, and the parameters are optional because the defaults are sensible: no customization string, and an output of 32 or 64 bytes. The value of L is fixed at 256 or 512 bits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document updates the CMS algorithms document, and the security considerations section of that document applies here as well. NIST has defined appropriate use of the hash functions in terms of algorithm strengths and expected time frames for secure use in its Special Publications, which can be used as guides to choose appropriate key sizes for various security scenarios.

SHAKE128 with an output length of 32 bytes offers 128 bits of collision and preimage resistance, so the SHAKE128 identifiers are RECOMMENDED with a 2048-bit RSA modulus, giving 112-bit security, or a 3072-bit modulus giving 128-bit security, or curves with a group order of 256 bits. SHAKE256 with a 64-byte output length offers 256 bits of collision and preimage resistance, so the SHAKE256 identifiers are RECOMMENDED with a 4096-bit RSA modulus or higher, or curves with a group order of at least 512 bits, such as NIST curve P-521, giving 256-bit security. The RFC notes that 4096-bit RSA is recommended because 256 bits of security would need a 15360-bit modulus, which is impractical for today's technology.

When more than two parties share the same message-authentication key, data origin authentication is not provided. Any party that knows the key can compute a valid MAC, so the content could have come from any one of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash length sets how much strength the signature has, so the key has to be big enough to match: a 32-byte SHAKE128 output works with a 2048-bit RSA key, and a 64-byte SHAKE256 output calls for a 4096-bit key or a large elliptic curve. The RFC also warns that a message authentication key shared between more than two parties proves nothing about who sent the message.
